description: Eastern white pines are an iconic tree to the northeastern US, especially New England, though they can be found west to Michigan and south to eastern Tennessee. The eastern white pine is the tallest tree east of the Mississippi, with the largest documented specimen reaching 174 feet in western MA. Most of the largest eastern white pines in New England were cut to make masts for British navy ships, as a consequence very few old trees survive. We are blessed to have some centuries old white pines here on the UNH campus (pictured here). Eastern white pines have 5 needles per bundle, the most of any pine in the northeast. Eastern white pines are often hit by the white pine weevil, a beetle that causes the original trunk to die, and as a consequence two or more trunks sprout in its place. Common neighbors of the eastern white pine include the eastern hemlock, northern red oak, shagbark hickory, and many, many others.

description: As I walked through the pine tree reserve on campus, I was quick to notice the variety of life scattered among the nature and specifically the rocks. Most importantly, I was fascinated by the amount of fungi present in this area. As I walked into this area next to campus, I first saw towering trees covered in lichen. However, I was quick to notice that the lichen only grew on the side of the tree where there was no sunlight and it was shaded. After taking a picture and walking around for 30 more minutes, I came across a rock and around this rock, there were mushrooms, a type of fungi. These mushrooms were white and scattered about two feet from each other. It seems as if they were connected and there roots were buried below the ground. What surprised me the most was the color, as the mushroom's top or tips were slightly brown colored. This could potentially mean that it could be lacking nutrients and might be dying. After seeing these mushrooms, I was quick to notice a whole new assortment of plants. Right next to the mushrooms, were an assortment of white dandelion plants. I was surprised by the close proximity of these plants to the mushrooms because mushroom's have very long roots. Anyways, the white dandelion plants seemed very delicate as their stem was very long and thin. This is surprising to see in an environment that withstands the brutal weather Boston  experiences. After walking around for 30 more minutes, I saw an accumulation of pine cones. There were there pine cones and each were brown and had lichen growing on their outer "shell." This was amazing to see because, pine cones can host a relationship between a variety of organisms. While there was green lichen growing on the pine cones, there were insects coming in and out of the cones as well. Lastly, as I was leaving the pine tree reserve on campus, I was quick to notice a huge rock that over half-way consumed by moss and lichen. I was amazed by how much lichen and moss was on this rock. It made sense for lichen and moss to be on the rock because there was no sunlight hitting this part of the pine tree reserve. The moss was extraordinarily green and the lichen was lighter green. Overall, I learned how amazing fungi can be.

description: In a large, mature, mostly publicly owned forest tract on a gradual north-facing slope, dominated by red oak and red maple, uncommon for Worcester County. Mature, tall white pine occurs  in small patches mostly on the east side, where 200 year old stone walls are prominent, some of which are double wide indicating formerly plowed fields and the presence of deeper, richer soil. An additional feature is the complete absence of woody invasive species. Mountain laurel and witch hazel are uncommon, in contrast to much of the surrounding area forests. White birch is more common than black birch, another unusual feature. White ash is occasional, some have been attacked by emerald ash borer and are dying out. *Pinus strobus* ("Whirling Pine"), Eastern White Pine

Eastern White Pines are found throughout the east, reaching it's furthest western point in Minnesota. This species is widely renowned as being one of North America's most historic tree species, but we'll get into that later.
White Pines can be identified with their shape, which are often oval-shaped from below and spikey-looking. It's needles occur in clusters of five, unlike *Pinus resinosa*, Red Pine, which occur in clumps of two. The cones are also whirly in shape (hence the scientific name) and elongated. Their bark is either only gray or brown to bronze while Red Pines are consistently gray with orange-red splotches from the bark flaking off.
So, back to what I stated earlier, for those of you who don't know, this tree played a role in shaping the United States into an independent nation from Great Britain back in the American Revolution. So, long story short, these trees were widely cut down for boat masts and the British King wanted to take these trees for himself, but this created tensions between the Brits and the Thirteen Colonies and became one motivator for the Colonies to revolt against Great Britain. That's how these giants had a role to shape the United States as an independent nation.
